entry.title: The 3.5-Point Win That Disappeared: Advancement vs. Acceleration

link.title: The 3.5-Point Win That Disappeared: Advancement vs. Acceleration

entry.content:
English / 中文

Designing Training Data for Language Models · Part 1 of 3
When to optimize, what makes data good, and how to change it.
Advancement vs. Acceleration · What Makes Training Data Good? · From Target to Operator

We had been trying to improve a language model’s capability by optimizing its training-data mixture. The hope was simple: if we allocated the token budget more intelligently across domains, perhaps the resulting model would become genuinely better.

For one experiment, following the setup from Aioli, we search for the optimal data mixture on seven SlimPajama domains—ArXiv, Books, C4, CommonCrawl, GitHub, StackExchange, and Wikipedia. We tried RegMix, which trains small proxy models on different mixtures, fits a regression model to their outcomes, and uses it to propose a promising mixture for a larger run. A fresh model is trained under that RegMix-optimized mixture after the optimal mixture is obtained.

At 2,000 training steps, this new model beat the one trained with a uniform mixture by 3.5 averaged-perplexity points. It looked like exactly the result we had hoped for. If we had stopped there—as fixed-budget comparisons often do—we would have called it a convincing success.

Then we kept the same run going, consuming more training data.

The gap shrank. And shrank. By the end, it was gone.

RegMix is 3.5 perplexity points better at 2,000 steps. At the final checkpoint it is slightly worse than Uniform: the important observation is not that the two runs become identical, but that RegMix no longer retains an advantage.

That disappearing win left me with a question that eventually became the focus of this work:

When data curation improves a language model, does it change what the model can ultimately learn, or only how quickly it gets there?

The result was real, but its meaning was narrower than the early checkpoint suggested. RegMix reached a given performance sooner without producing a better attainable model.

This is where I find a lot of discussion around data curation surprisingly slippery. We use the word improvement for two different things:

Acceleration changes how quickly we reach a level of performance.
Advancement changes the best level of performance we can eventually reach.

Acceleration can be valuable in its own right: reaching the same capability with substantially fewer tokens is a meaningful gain. Here, though, I am interested in a different question: can changing the training data improve the attainable endpoint? The disappearing advantage in our experiment made that distinction worth examining.

The endpoint and the road to it

Let $\mathcal E_\alpha(w)$ denote target performance after training with data budget $\alpha$ under curation policy $w$. The policy may represent domain-mixture weights, example-selection decisions, or token-level masks. To keep the inequalities concrete, write $\mathcal E$ in a lower-is-better orientation—loss, error, or negative accuracy. For an accuracy metric, simply reverse the inequalities.

The endpoint is

\[\mathcal E_\infty(w)=\lim_{\alpha\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal E_\alpha(w).\]

A policy provides advancement if

\[\mathcal E_\infty(w)<\mathcal E_\infty(w_0),\]

where $w_0$ indicates the uncurated baseline.

For a target performance level $\varepsilon$, let $\alpha_w(\varepsilon)$ be the smallest budget needed to reach it. The policy provides acceleration if

\[\alpha_w(\varepsilon)<\alpha_{w_0}(\varepsilon).\]

Acceleration changes the road: the same performance is reached with less data. Advancement changes the destination: the endpoint itself improves. A single checkpoint cannot distinguish the two.

Why would a data method change the endpoint at all?

Suppose I give you a gigantic jar containing red and blue marbles and ask you to reproduce the same red–blue ratio in another jar. A clever sampling strategy may help you estimate the ratio faster. But if ordinary sampling already targets the right distribution, no reweighting trick should produce a more correct answer in the limit.

Data curation has the same basic constraint. Write it as a bilevel problem:

\[\min_w \; \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}\!\left(\theta^*(w)\right) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \theta^*(w)\in\arg\min_\theta \mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w).\]

The inner problem optimizes the model parameters $\theta$. The outer problem optimizes the data policy $w$, which determines the trained model $\theta^(w)$. But if the uncurated training objective already *matches the target objective, where could a better endpoint come from?

The one-line obstruction

Let $w_0$ denote the uncurated baseline and suppose, crucially, that there is no train–target gap at the population level:

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta;w_0) = \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta) \qquad \text{for every }\theta.\]

“Matches” means that, under the baseline policy $w_0$, training and target losses are the same function of $\theta$—not just equal at one checkpoint. These are population losses: expectations over the underlying data distributions. In the idealized large-data limit $\alpha\to\infty$, converged training minimizes this objective.

When the inner optimization converges, the baseline solution

\[\theta^*(w_0)\in\arg\min_\theta \mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta;w_0)\]

also globally minimizes the target objective—because, under $w_0$, the training and target losses are the same function. For any alternative curation policy $w$, its trained solution $\theta^*(w)$ is still another model in the same hypothesis class. Therefore

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{pop}}\!\left(\theta^*(w_0)\right) = \min_\theta \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta) \leq \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{pop}}\!\left(\theta^*(w)\right).\]

That is the obstruction: when the uncurated baseline already optimizes the target population objective, no reallocation can produce a strictly better target endpoint. This conclusion assumes a fixed model class and converged inner optimization.

The argument is simple, but its implication is easy to overlook in practice. When a better mixture or subset wins at a finite training budget, it is tempting to read that gain as evidence of a better endpoint. Yet without a correctable population gap, the gain can be acceleration alone.

A mixture example. For $K$ domains, let $w_k$ be domain $k$’s training proportion and $\widehat w_k$ its fixed importance in the target. Both weight vectors are nonnegative and sum to one. The population objectives are

\[\begin{aligned} &\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta;w) =\sum_{k=1}^K w_k\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^{k,\mathrm{pop}}(\theta),\\ &\mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta) =\sum_{k=1}^K\widehat w_k\mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}^{k,\mathrm{pop}}(\theta). \end{aligned}\]

The training proportions $w$ are the decision. If training and target share the same distribution within each domain and $w_0=\widehat w$, their population objectives are identical—the no-gap condition above.

This is the population picture behind abundant, single-pass training when training and evaluation data are sampled i.i.d. from the same underlying distribution: more data makes the empirical objectives approach the same expected loss.

The seven-domain SlimPajama experiment above uses equal target weights, $\widehat w_k=1/K=1/7$. Its uniform baseline therefore has $w_{0,k}=\widehat w_k$. When training and evaluation sample the same underlying distribution within each domain, this baseline already minimizes the target objective at the population endpoint. The early gains in those learning curves are therefore consistent with acceleration. This remains true even when some domains are harder to learn than others. Giving harder domains more weight may help at finite budgets, but difficulty differences alone do not create room for a better endpoint when the baseline already matches the target.

These results are developed in our paper, Advancement or Acceleration? How Data Curation Improves LLM Training.

Lasting advancement requires a correctable train–target gap.

A train–target gap leaves room for advancement, but does not guarantee it. The available data and the way we can change its use must allow us to reduce that gap. This is what correctable means here.

Seeing acceleration and advancement

To make the distinction concrete, we use teacher–student perceptron models: a teacher generates labels, and a student learns from the curated data (see Loureiro et al., 2021 for learning-curve analysis and Sorscher et al., 2022 for data pruning). These models let us study both learning at finite data budgets and the $\alpha\to\infty$ endpoint, distinguishing gains that fade from those that persist. The technical derivations are given in the paper.

Read the figure by rows: mixture above, selection below. The left column shows the setup, the middle shows acceleration without a gap, and the right shows what changes when a gap is present. Here $\alpha=P/N$ measures the data budget in samples per parameter.

Mixture: reweighting can accelerate learning without a gap—and improve the endpoint when it corrects one. To illustrate acceleration, we make domain 2 harder to learn than domain 1 in the top row (see the paper for the construction). The training proportion of domain 1 is $w_1$ and its target weight is $\widehat w_1=0.5$. When $w_1 = \widehat w_1=0.5$(no gap), giving the harder domain more training data helps at small budgets, but the advantage disappears as the budget grows (b). When the target weights change, the best mixture changes with them: panel (c) shows that target matching is optimal at a large but finite budget. In the paper, we further show that this optimality holds as $\alpha\to\infty$, even when domain difficulty differs.

Selection: pruning can accelerate learning without a gap—and improve the endpoint when it corrects one. In the bottom row, we construct the training and target labeling rules using two linear perceptron teachers. Each is described by a vector normal to its decision boundary: $B$ for training and $B_{\mathrm{tar}}$ for the target. The angle $\phi$ between them controls the train–target mismatch (d). The retained fraction is $f$, so $f=1$ means keeping everything. We select examples using a criterion that favors those near the target decision boundary and penalizes those whose training labels disagree with the target teacher. Without a gap, moderate pruning can preserve accuracy with less data, but cannot improve the endpoint (e). With a gap, selection trades off fewer training examples against better alignment with the target. Panel (f) shows that the alignment benefit can outweigh the loss of data. In the paper, we show that the gain can persist as $\alpha\to\infty$.

In the top row, lower target loss is better. In the bottom row, higher target accuracy is better. The selection plots run from full retention on the left to stronger pruning on the right. Solid lines are theoretical predictions and circles are simulations with $N=200$.

A one-run diagnostic before an expensive search

The population condition is clean but cannot usually be checked directly on real corpora. We therefore use the $\Delta$-test as an observable diagnostic from an ordinary uncurated baseline run. Let $\theta$ denote a model checkpoint from that run; the diagnostic does not require training to have converged.

For a $K$-domain mixture,

\[\Delta = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left| \widehat w_k\mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}^k\!\left(\theta\right) - w_{0,k}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^k\!\left(\theta\right) \right|.\]

Here $\widehat w_k$ is domain $k$’s importance in the target distribution, while $w_{0,k}$ is its exposure under the uncurated training mixture.

For selection, there is a single candidate pool, so the diagnostic reduces to

\[\Delta = \left| \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}\!\left(\theta\right) - \mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}\!\left(\theta\right) \right|,\]

where $w_0$ means full retention.

In our experiments, the $\Delta$-test provides a useful early signal: appreciably nonzero values indicate opportunities for persistent gains, while gains near $\Delta=0$ tend to fade as the budget grows. A near-zero $\Delta$ suggests limited headroom, though it does not rule out every train–target gap. Note that $\Delta$ is not a sufficient condition for advancement: the available data and policy still determine whether the detected gap can be corrected.

Controlled interventions on the gap

We tested two questions in both mixture and selection experiments: do curation gains depend on the train–target gap, and can the $\Delta$-test identify promising tasks before an expensive search? We varied the train–target gap while keeping the methods and training setup largely unchanged.

The experiments below track gains within the training budgets we tested; the infinite-data conclusions come from the analysis above. The reported $\Delta$ values are measured halfway through the uncurated baseline’s training budget, rather than after full convergence. In practice, we can use a small proxy model for diagnosis before larger runs to reduce additional computation.

For mixture, we compared Uniform with Skill-It, RegMix, Aioli, DoGE, and TANDEM:

  • Matched regime ($\Delta=0.07$). This is the seven-domain SlimPajama setting from the opening experiment. Training and target weight the domains equally, and the pool is large enough to avoid repeatedly sampling depleted domains. Final averaged perplexities ranged from 19.66 to 20.17, statistically close to Uniform at 19.71. By the final checkpoint, the early leads had disappeared within experimental variation.
  • Endogenous gap ($\Delta=0.64$). We keep the same uniformly weighted target but restrict the pool to 300M tokens, preserving its original domain proportions. Small domains such as ArXiv and Wikipedia run out early and are repeatedly sampled. Overfitting lowers their training losses relative to held-out target losses: the gap is endogenous because it develops through training on limited data. Optimized mixtures improve performance by reducing exposure to these overfit domains.
  • Exogenous gap ($\Delta=1.26$). We hold out CommonCrawl as the target and train on the remaining six domains. The gap is exogenous because the target distribution differs from the candidate training pool. Related data such as C4 still offers a way to partially correct the mismatch by reweighting. Target perplexity fell from 49.19 under Uniform to roughly 40–41 under optimized mixtures.

The same mixture methods produce negligible gains by the final checkpoint in the approximately matched regime, while gains remain through the largest tested budget in settings with correctable gaps.

Selection provides a paired control. We kept the model, 5B-token OpenWebMath candidate pool, 60% keep ratio, and training protocol fixed. We compared Random, EL2N, InfoBatch, Token-Cleaning, RHO-1, and BLADE, alongside full-pool continual training. Using the same methods in both settings, we changed only the target used for selection and evaluation.

  • With an in-distribution OpenWebMath target, $\Delta=0.016$ and no selector consistently beat full-pool continual training.
  • With a shifted MetaMath–MAmmoTH target, $\Delta=0.549$. Target-aware RHO-1 and BLADE could now correct a visible mismatch. BLADE raised average benchmark accuracy from 17.21 to 31.31 while retaining 60% of the candidate tokens.

Selection yields little improvement over full-pool continual training in the approximately matched setting, but substantial gains with a correctable gap. The $\Delta$-test distinguishes these settings before selection.

A different order of operations

These results suggest that before asking which curation method to use, we should ask what improvement the task leaves room for. The $\Delta$-test offers a practical starting point for that diagnosis.

A common data curation workflow begins with the method:

  1. Invent a data-utility scoring rule.
  2. Select or reweight data.
  3. Train a model.
  4. Hope the target metric improves.

I would instead start with the task:

  1. Define the target. What distribution and metrics represent the capability we actually care about?
  2. Run the uncurated reference and diagnose the task. Estimate $\Delta$ with a small proxy when possible.
  3. Check correctability. Does the candidate pool contain the missing modes, and can mixture or selection expose them?
  4. Specify the claim and optimize the data. Are we trying to save compute, move the attainable endpoint, or both?
  5. Validate accordingly. For acceleration, report tokens, FLOPs, or wall-clock time at matched performance. For advancement, increase the budget and test whether the advantage persists.

Reaching the same capability with less compute and improving the attainable endpoint are both useful. They answer different questions and call for different evaluations. In either case, the value of changing the data depends on the target. This raises a further question: can training data be called “high quality” before we specify what we want the learner to achieve?

That is the subject of the next essay.

entry.title: What Makes Training Data Good? Quality, Diversity, and the Missing Target

link.title: What Makes Training Data Good? Quality, Diversity, and the Missing Target

entry.content:
English / 中文

Designing Training Data for Language Models · Part 2 of 3
When to optimize, what makes data good, and how to change it.
Advancement vs. Acceleration · What Makes Training Data Good? · From Target to Operator

Imagine two training examples.

The first is a beautifully written encyclopedia article: clean grammar, reliable facts, coherent structure. The second is an ugly scratchpad from a failed geometry proof: abbreviations, backtracking, half-finished equations, and one crucial correction near the end.

Which one is better data?

For a general-purpose language model, perhaps the first. For a model that must recover from mistakes in mathematical reasoning, perhaps the second. For a product-description generator, probably neither.

“Good data depends on the task” is not a surprising claim. The problem is that many pipelines cease to behave as if it were true once a proxy score is treated as an intrinsic property of the data. Much of data engineering starts by asking whether a sample is “high quality,” as if quality were printed somewhere inside it. We try to uncover that quality with heuristic rules, reference language models, learned classifiers, and LLM judges. We then add diversity so that the high-scoring set does not become too narrow.

This recipe often works. But the language hides two missing variables:

Quality according to whom—and diversity over what?

“Quality” is too vague to optimize

Suppose the raw pool follows $p_{\mathrm{pool}}(x)$, and a quality score induces a selection weight or acceptance probability $w(x)$. After filtering, we train on

\[q(x) = \frac{p_{\mathrm{pool}}(x)w(x)} {\int p_{\mathrm{pool}}(x')w(x')\,dx'}.\]

The scorer has not discovered a label attached to each sample by nature. It has changed the probability with which the learner sees different regions of the pool. But the literature gives strikingly different answers about which examples should receive more of that mass.

This ambiguity is obvious in how quality scores treat “difficulty”.

Sometimes, hard examples are good:

  • high-loss samples carry more learning signal;
  • small-margin samples refine a decision boundary;
  • frequently forgotten samples reveal unstable knowledge;
  • examples with large gradients promise a larger parameter update.

Sometimes, easy examples are good:

  • low-loss samples are less likely to be mislabeled;
  • confident examples are safer for self-training;
  • simple examples may support a curriculum.

Both recipes can be reasonable, yet they push probability mass in opposite directions. The word quality has not resolved the disagreement; it has merely been attached to both.

Connection to Part 1. Difficulty-based scores may improve efficiency or robustness, but without an external target signal they do not by themselves identify the direction of a train–target gap. In the language of the previous essay, they are more natural guides to acceleration than to stable advancement.

Successful filters often implicitly encode a target distribution

Many successful filters do not measure quality in the abstract. They implicitly define a target distribution over data, then favor examples that receive higher probability or preference under that distribution.

CCNet uses a KenLM model trained on Wikipedia to score web documents. Low perplexity means that a document resembles the reference language distribution. The resulting filter moves a broad web crawl toward Wikipedia-like text.

DataComp-LM makes this dependence especially visible. Its fastText filter contrasts a positive corpus with broad web data. Changing that positive corpus—from Wikipedia or OpenWebText to OpenHermes plus highly rated ExplainLikeImFive answers—changes what the classifier seeks; the latter produced the strongest filter in its ablation.

LLM-based pipelines induce a preference distribution through a rubric-conditioned judge. QuRating, AlpaGasus, and DEITA turn different prompts, judges, and criteria into different accepted distributions.

Viewed this way, a Wikipedia-trained language model, a classifier trained on a preferred corpus, and a rubric-conditioned LLM judge are different ways of parameterizing the same object: an implicit target distribution over training examples. Hence these methods work not because they uncover universal quality, but because their proxy distributions point in a useful direction.

Connection to Part 1. These filters are most likely to yield stable gains when the target distribution they encode is better aligned with the downstream target than the original training pool. In that case, filtering is not discovering universal quality; it is closing an existing train–target gap. Their success is therefore consistent with the gap view of advancement developed in the previous essay.

Nevertheless, agreement with a proxy distribution is not evidence of downstream value. The proxy must be aligned with the downstream target, and that alignment can only be validated through the model trained on the shifted distribution. Even when the direction is correct, most quality scoring remains pointwise: it ignores relationships among examples and can spend a finite data budget repeatedly selecting near-duplicates, leaving the resulting dataset too narrow.

Diversity is the intuitive patch—but diversity in what?

Diversity is the natural patch for this pointwise failure. It makes selection aware of the set, not just each example in isolation, and can discourage a high-scoring subset from collapsing around redundant examples.

But like quality, diversity is a meta-property rather than a concrete selection criterion. It becomes computable only after choosing what counts as different. A geometric coreset covers an embedding space; cluster-based selection such as DEITA spreads examples across neighborhoods; a determinantal point process rewards separation under its kernel. Each can be principled once its geometry is fixed, but different geometries preserve different distinctions: topic embeddings may cover subjects while missing reasoning difficulty, whereas gradient representations group examples by their effect on training. A choice that works for one target need not transfer to another.

The ambiguity becomes larger when diversity is combined with quality. We can filter by quality and then diversify, select the highest-scoring example from each cluster, or optimize a weighted combination of the two. These procedures need not select the same data, and “quality plus diversity” provides no common scale or target-derived rule for choosing among them.

Quality can propose a direction, and diversity can guard against redundancy. But their combination neither supplies a target-derived trade-off nor evaluates the model that the chosen distribution will produce.

From scoring samples to optimizing a training distribution

The direct formulation is bilevel: choose a training distribution by evaluating the model it produces on the downstream target.

\[\min_{q\in\mathcal Q} \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}\!\left(\theta^*(q)\right) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \theta^*(q) \in \arg\min_\theta \mathbb E_{x\sim q}[\ell(x;\theta)].\]

The inner problem maps a training distribution $q$ to a trained model $\theta^*(q)$. The outer problem compares candidate distributions by evaluating those models on the downstream target. The decision variable is the distribution as a whole, not a collection of permanent sample scores.

This makes the missing interaction explicit. The value of assigning more probability to one region depends on what else has already been selected and on how the learner responds to the resulting allocation. A pointwise quality score ignores this interaction. A diversity term can partially account for redundancy, but only under the geometry induced by the chosen representation. The bilevel objective instead evaluates the allocation as a whole through the model it produces.

Reachability still matters

The bilevel objective tells us how to compare training distributions, but not which distributions are reachable. Selection can only reweight or remove examples already in a candidate pool. If a needed capability is absent, the remedy is retrieval, collection, or synthesis—not a better ranking score.

More generally, the feasible set $\mathcal Q$ is defined by the data operator and its budget. Mixture redistributes mass across predefined groups, selection acts within an existing pool, and synthesis can expand its support. The target determines how reachable distributions are evaluated; the operator and budget determine which distributions can be considered at all. The next essay shows how mixture, selection, and synthesis instantiate different feasible sets within the same bilevel formulation—and how the resulting optimization problems can be approached.

What, then, is good data?

Some decisions remain straightforward: remove invalid files, exact duplicates, or verified label errors. Beyond such hygiene, however, “good” is not a property of an example in isolation. It describes the role that example plays alongside the rest of the training distribution for a target.

I would not replace “quality and diversity” with another slogan. The more useful question is:

Given a target, a training procedure, a budget, and a feasible family of training distributions $\mathcal Q$, which $q\in\mathcal Q$ produces the model we prefer?

Quality scores can supply useful signals, and diversity can protect coverage. But they are proxies or constraints within this decision, not target-independent definitions of training value.

Good data, then, is not a universal subset waiting to be discovered. It is a training distribution to be designed for a target.

entry.title: From Target to Operator: Mixture, Selection, and Synthesis

link.title: From Target to Operator: Mixture, Selection, and Synthesis

entry.content:
English / 中文

Designing Training Data for Language Models · Part 3 of 3
When to optimize, what makes data good, and how to change it.
Advancement vs. Acceleration · What Makes Training Data Good? · From Target to Operator

Suppose we want a language model to perform better on a target—a domain, a task, or a set of capabilities—and can change the data it trains on. Which changes should we make?

One objective, three operators

A direct way to pose the problem is to choose a training distribution $q$ by evaluating the model $\theta^*(q)$ it produces on the target. Let $\mathcal Q$ be the family of training distributions available to us. This gives a bilevel objective:

\[\min_{q\in\mathcal Q} \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}\!\left(\theta^*(q)\right) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \theta^*(q)\in\arg\min_\theta \mathbb E_{x\sim q}[\ell(x;\theta)].\]

The inner problem trains the model on $q$. The outer problem chooses that distribution to improve the trained model’s target performance.

The previous essay develops the motivation for this view. Here, we turn to the “how”: what changes can we make to the training data, and how can we find changes that move us toward that goal? The first concerns the data operator, and the second concerns the solver.

Three common operators are to adjust the proportions of data from different domains (mixture), choose examples or tokens from an existing pool (selection), or generate new training examples (synthesis).

Operator Decision variable What it can change Its boundary
Mixture Domain proportions Exposure across predefined groups Cannot distinguish examples inside a group
Selection Example or token weights Exposure within an existing pool Cannot create a missing mode
Synthesis Generator, prompt, or task specification The examples available for training Does not guarantee useful or correct data

Each operator defines a different feasible family $\mathcal Q$. Mixture and selection change exposure within existing data. If a useful behavior is present but rare, reallocating exposure may help. If the required training material is absent, we need to collect or generate it. Synthesis lets us change which examples are available, extending distribution design beyond reallocation.

Choosing an operator gives us a set of decisions—domain proportions, token masks, or generation choices. For a given operator, we still need to optimize its decision variables. The most literal approach is to propose a mixture, train a language model, evaluate it on the target, and repeat until the compute budget, or our patience, runs out. Trying every possible subset for selection is even less inviting. Can we optimize these data decisions without solving the training problem from scratch for every candidate?

From the bilevel objective to an allocation update

This section explains how the penalty reformulation leads to the allocation update. If you prefer the intuition behind the update rules, you can skip ahead to the sections below: TANDEM: which domains deserve more exposure? and BLADE: which tokens deserve the budget?. These explain how the resulting update rules adjust domain weights or select tokens.

We first consider mixture and selection, where the decision is how to allocate training exposure within existing data. Let $w$ denote these allocation variables and $\mathcal W$ their feasible set. For mixture, $w_k$ is the sampling proportion of domain $k$; for selection, $w_p$ is the selection weight of candidate $p$. Their dimensions and constraints differ, but both induce a training distribution $q_w$.

Writing $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w)=\mathbb E_{x\sim q_w}[\ell(x;\theta)]$, we can express the same bilevel objective in terms of $w$. We use $\theta^*(w)$ as shorthand for the model trained on $q_w$. Synthesis will require a different parameterization, which we return to below.

We use a penalty reformulation to turn the coupled bilevel problem into a single-level optimization problem. Let $V(w)=\min_\theta\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w)$ be the minimum training loss under allocation $w$. We penalize the excess training loss above this minimum:

\[H_\lambda(w,\theta) =\mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}(\theta) +\lambda\left[ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w)-V(w) \right], \qquad\lambda>0.\]

The target term encourages low target loss, while the penalty encourages the model to approximately satisfy the inner training constraint. This construction introduces two model roles: a proxy, trained to approximate the minimum in $V(w)$, and a reference, trained on target loss plus a weighted training loss. Their ideal optimization targets are:

\[\begin{aligned} &\theta_{\mathrm{proxy}}^*(w) \in\arg\min_\theta\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w),\\ &\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}^*(w) \in\arg\min_\theta\left[ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}(\theta) +\lambda\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w) \right]. \end{aligned}\]

The algorithms coordinate updates of the two models and the allocation. The proxy parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{proxy}}$ take gradient steps on training loss, while the reference parameters $\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ take steps on target loss plus the weighted training loss. Both use a finite number of steps to approximate the minimization problems above.

For the allocation update, we hold $\theta_{\mathrm{proxy}}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}$ fixed and use the proxy to approximate the inner minimum. We then differentiate the resulting loss contrast with respect to $w$:

\[\begin{aligned} &\partial_w\left\{\lambda\left[ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta_{\mathrm{ref}};w) -\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta_{\mathrm{proxy}};w) \right]\right\}\\ &=\lambda\left[ \partial_w\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta_{\mathrm{ref}};w) -\partial_w\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta_{\mathrm{proxy}};w) \right]. \end{aligned}\]

For the specific mixture and selection formulations outlined in the next two sections, training loss is linear in $w$. The allocation update therefore reduces to the loss difference:

\[s_i= \mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^i(\theta_{\mathrm{proxy}}) -\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^i(\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}).\]

Here $i$ indexes domains for mixture and tokens for selection. The allocation gradient estimate is proportional to $-s_i$, so descent favors larger $s_i$, subject to the operator’s constraints.

The shared penalty-based solver for mixture and selection. Two coupled models produce a loss-difference update signal; the operator’s constraints determine the resulting allocation rule.

TANDEM: which domains deserve more exposure?

Suppose we can adjust how often the learner sees each of $K$ domains. Here $w_k$ is the probability of sampling domain $k$, and $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^k(\theta)$ is the model’s expected training loss on that domain. The shared bilevel formulation takes the following concrete form:

Component TANDEM
Target loss A weighted average of held-out losses across domains. The target weights $\widehat w_k$ specify each domain’s contribution to evaluation (typically, $\widehat w_k=1/K$). These weights stay fixed while the training proportions $w$ are optimized.
Training loss $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w)=\sum_{k=1}^K w_k\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^k(\theta)$.
Feasible allocations Domain proportions on the probability simplex $\mathcal W_{\mathrm{mix}}$: $w_k\geq0$ and $\sum_k w_k=1$.

The training loss shows the linear dependence on $w$ used in the shared solver: each domain weight multiplies its domain loss. Differentiating with respect to $w_k$ therefore returns $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^k(\theta)$. This is why the shared solver’s difference of training-loss derivatives becomes a difference of domain losses between the reference and proxy, giving the allocation gradient estimate $-\lambda s_k$. A projected-gradient step turns it into a new mixture:

\[w^{(t+1)} =\Pi_{\mathcal W_{\mathrm{mix}}} \left(w^{(t)}+\eta_w\lambda s^{(t)}\right).\]

At the domain level, a larger positive $s_k$ means that incorporating target information has improved predictions on domain $k$: the reference has lower domain loss than the training-only proxy. The update gives such domains upward pressure in the training mixture. Projection keeps the probabilities nonnegative and summing to one. The learned mixture is then used to train a fresh final model.

In practice, TANDEM synchronizes the two models to control their separation and stabilize optimization, while scheduling updates to reduce search cost. The paper provides the full procedure and a first-order stationarity guarantee under its stated assumptions; see Section 2.2 and Appendix A in TANDEM.

For a concrete result, consider the data-restricted SlimPajama experiment: a 160M model trained from a 300M-token candidate corpus, with smaller domains repeatedly sampled. TANDEM’s learned mixture reduces averaged perplexity from 31.53 under Uniform to 28.07, under the same final-training protocol. Here averaged perplexity is the exponential of the mean held-out domain loss.

What initially surprised me was how little there was to gain in the data-abundant, single-pass pretraining: TANDEM achieved an averaged perplexity of 25.43, compared with 25.74 under Uniform. In this experiment, both Uniform training and target evaluation assign weight $1/K$ to each domain, and their within-domain data come from the same underlying distributions. The population objectives therefore match. Abundant data allows training without repeated exposure to individual samples, and the observed train–validation gaps remain close to zero. Later, the work discussed in Part 1 helped make sense of this contrast: this matched regime leaves little distributional mismatch for reweighting to correct. The solver was effective, but the task offered limited headroom for advancement.

BLADE: which tokens deserve the budget?

A domain is a blunt unit of intervention. Useful and unhelpful material can occur in the same document, or even the same reasoning trace. We therefore move the allocation decision down to individual tokens. Here $w_p$ indicates whether candidate token $p$ contributes to training: one means retained, zero means masked. $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^p(\theta)$ is then the prediction loss at token position $p$. For a pool of $P$ candidates, we retain a fraction $f$. The shared bilevel formulation takes the following concrete form:

Component BLADE
Target loss Prediction loss on the target validation data, $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}(\theta)$.
Training loss Average loss over retained token positions: $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta;w)=\frac{1}{fP}\sum_{p=1}^P w_p\mathcal L_{\mathrm{train}}^p(\theta)$.
Feasible allocations A token mask with $w_p\in\lbrace 0,1\rbrace$ and $\sum_p w_p=fP$.

The training loss shows the same linear dependence on $w$, so the shared solver gives a token-level loss-difference update, with allocation gradient estimate $-\lambda s_p/(fP)$. To optimize the binary mask, we relax $w_p\in\lbrace 0,1\rbrace$ to $w_p\in[0,1]$, keeping the same budget. The resulting feasible set is a capped simplex.

In TANDEM, domain proportions are continuous probabilities constrained to sum to one, so we use projected gradient descent to keep each update within the simplex. BLADE instead requires a keep-or-discard decision for each token. We temporarily allow fractional token weights to make this discrete problem amenable to continuous optimization. Frank–Wolfe then gives an elegant result: with a full, greedy step, the update lands directly on a binary mask—the $fP$ tokens with the largest loss-difference scores—with no extra rounding needed:

\[w_p =\mathbf 1\left\{p\in\operatorname{Top}_{fP}(s)\right\}.\]

The token-level loss difference reflects the predictive improvement associated with target-informed training, providing a signal for which tokens may help align the learner with the target. To make this criterion practical at corpus scale, BLADE applies the selection rule within candidate batches, enabling online token selection without scoring and storing the entire corpus in advance.

We evaluate token selection by continually pretraining a 13B language model on a 5B-token OpenWebMath pool. Across nine math-related benchmarks, BLADE achieves 54.4% average accuracy, compared with 52.5% for RHO-1 and 43.7% for full-pool continual pretraining. BLADE and RHO-1 each retain 3B loss-bearing tokens, while full-pool training uses all 5B tokens.

BLADE connects the bilevel foundation of influence-based selection with the practical loss-difference criterion of RHO-style methods, while introducing a dynamic reference synchronized with the learner. The penalty formulation provides this connection using first-order model updates and loss evaluations, without the inverse-Hessian computations associated with classical influence functions. The reference is periodically refreshed from the proxy and updated with target information, keeping the comparison tied to the learner rather than a fixed pretrained reference. See Section 2.3 for the relationship between the methods. The analyzed full-coordinate procedure also has a first-order stationarity guarantee under the assumptions and parameter choices in Appendix A.

TANDEM and BLADE use the same proxy/reference construction to update training exposure. The constraints turn that update into domain proportions in one case and a Top-$k$ token mask in the other. The loss-difference update depends jointly on the target and the learned states of the proxy and reference models. These states reflect the learning procedure and the combined effect of the training examples, including how their learning signals overlap or complement one another. This makes the perspective of Part 2 concrete: the criterion evaluates data through a learner and a target, rather than assigning each domain or token an intrinsic quality score.

Synthesis: when reallocation is not enough

Both data mixture and selection assume useful training material is somewhere in the pool. What if it is not? A curator cannot recover an absent tool-use example, failure-recovery pattern, or reasoning strategy. Synthesis lets us make the examples themselves part of the decision.

As with mixture and selection, synthesis is evaluated by the target performance of the model trained on the resulting data. The distribution-level objective remains the same, but its parameterization changes. Let $\psi$ control a generator, its prompts, or its task specifications, inducing a training distribution $q_\psi$. Writing $\theta^*(\psi)$ for the model trained on $q_\psi$, the problem becomes

\[\min_{\psi\in\Psi} \mathcal L_{\mathrm{target}}\!\left(\theta^*(\psi)\right) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \theta^*(\psi)\in\arg\min_\theta \mathbb E_{x\sim q_\psi}[\ell(x;\theta)].\]

The permitted generation parameters $\Psi$ and the generation budget define the reachable family $\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{synth}}={q_\psi:\psi\in\Psi}$. Generation can introduce missing modes or add examples within existing ones.

For mixture and selection, the training loss depends linearly on the allocation weights, yielding a simple loss-difference update. Whether an equally simple and efficient update can be obtained when the decision changes the generated examples themselves remains an open question for extending this solver to synthesis.

These operators, mixture, selection and synthesis, can also work together in a target-driven data pipeline. One practical loop I use is:

Target failures → identify missing training material → generate candidates → select or verify → train the model → evaluate on the target.

In this loop, an LLM generates candidates and target-guided selection determines what to retain, bypassing the need to solve the bilevel generation problem.

Target, Gap and operator

Across these three essays, the questions have moved from what kind of improvement we obtained, to what makes a training distribution valuable, to how we can change it in practice.

For a new data problem, the starting questions are what target matters, where ordinary training falls short, and whether the available data contains material that can help. These answers guide the choice of operator and how to optimize it.

Or, in three lines:

Target defines the objective.
Gap defines the headroom.
Operator defines the reachable improvement.

Data design begins when those three are specified together.
